question: What is the normal core body temperature range for a healthy person?
explanation: A healthy human core temperature stays steady between 36.5°C and 37.5°C to keep the body functioning at its best. [learn more](BMP111_U4_T5#BMP111_U4_T5_h1)

question: What is the main role of the skin in regulating body temperature?

options.A: It blocks all heat exchange between the body and the air.
options.B: It detects changes in the environment and helps the body respond.
options.C: It produces all the heat needed to keep internal organs warm.
options.D: It controls the nervous system signals that dictate metabolism.

explanation: The skin contains sensors and blood vessels that help sense outside temperatures and adjust how much heat the body loses or keeps. [learn more](BMP111_U4_T5#BMP111_U4_T5_h1)

question: Which part of the brain acts as the body's main thermostat?
explanation: The hypothalamus monitors core temperature and coordinates the body's heating and cooling systems. [learn more](BMP111_U4_T5#BMP111_U4_T5_h2)

question: Where do thermal receptors in the body send their primary temperature signals?

options.A: Straight to the peripheral blood vessels
options.B: To the skeletal muscles for shivering
options.C: Directly to the sweat glands in the skin
options.D: To the hypothalamus in the brain

explanation: Temperature sensors all over the body send data back to the hypothalamus so it can take action to keep the body comfortable. [learn more](BMP111_U4_T5#BMP111_U4_T5_h2)

question: What happens to surface blood vessels when the body needs to lose extra heat?
explanation: Widening the surface blood vessels brings warm blood closer to the skin so extra heat can escape into the air. [learn more](BMP111_U4_T5#BMP111_U4_T5_h3)

question: Which process makes sweating effective at cooling down an overheated body?

options.A: The chemical absorption of body fat by sweat
options.B: The freezing of water droplets on the skin
options.C: The evaporation of moisture from the skin
options.D: The direct contact of sweat with cool surfaces

explanation: As sweat turns from liquid to gas during evaporation, it absorbs and removes heat from the body. [learn more](BMP111_U4_T5#BMP111_U4_T5_h3)

question: Which of the following is NOT a way the body conserves or generates heat?
explanation: Sweating cools the body down rather than warming it up, so the body stops sweating when it is cold. [learn more](BMP111_U4_T5#BMP111_U4_T5_h4)

question: Why does a person start shivering after being in the cold for a long time?

options.A: The skin is shedding layers to trap warm air.
options.B: Surface blood vessels are widening to release energy.
options.C: The sweat glands are trying to cool the core.

explanation: Rapid, involuntary muscle shaking increases metabolism and generates internal heat to fight off the cold. [learn more](BMP111_U4_T5#BMP111_U4_T5_h4)

question: What skin condition often happens when a person has a rising fever?

options.A: Severe localized narrowing of blood vessels

explanation: As the body tries to release extra heat during a fever, blood vessels open up and sweat glands become active, making the skin warm and flushed. [learn more](BMP111_U4_T5#BMP111_U4_T5_h5)

question: Why is it important for a midwife to note how a patient's temperature was measured?

options.A: Different body sites give slightly different baseline temperature readings.
options.B: Armpit readings are always higher than internal core values.
options.C: The brain only responds to temperatures taken in the ear.
options.D: Only oral thermometers can detect hypothermia.

explanation: Sites like the mouth, ear, and armpit measure temperature a little differently, so clinicians account for these variations during assessment. [learn more](BMP111_U4_T5#BMP111_U4_T5_h5)
